Posted February 17, 2003
Analysis by Richard Cowan
See
The Medical Marijuana Problems -- Analysis by Richard Cowan

There has been an unofficial slow-motion race between the Dutch and Canadian governments to see which one would have the first real government medical cannabis program. The Dutch are winning. (The private Mediwiet program run by coffee-shop owners does not count, except for the patients.)
See
The Dutch To Begin Distributing Medical Cannabis Through Pharmacies. Health Canada Appeals Court Order To Do Same, But Wants to Call It Research. They Are Confusing. We Are Winning!

Actually, the Dutch had a program which allowed distribution through pharmacies in the early 1990s but killed it. Then they began to revive it in 1999, when they announced the formation of National Cannabis Agency which was to oversee the medical cannabis program.See
Dutch National Cannabis Agency To Be Launched
To Regulate Cannabis Production for Medical And Scientific Purposes

Then in April of 2001 the Canadians moved into the lead by announcing their program, but it really did very little to help the patients.
See
We Are Winning! Canadian Medical Marijuana Program: Politically Very Important, Medically and Scientifically Absurd.
and
Marijuana as Medicine and the Law Circa 2001 -- By John W. Conroy, QC --Unabridged Version Special to MarijuanaNews

Then, a month later, the Dutch moved back into contention with the announcement that " rijkshennep " royal official cannabis would be available in pharmacies, but they were getting ahead of themselves. It really did not quite happen on a scale that would help patients. (Sometimes the Dutch system can be so opaque that they are not sure what they are doing themselves!)
See
The Dutch Start Making Whole Cannabis Available By Prescription. Radio Netherlands Describes How Coffee Shops Work. -- 2 Items

When then Health Minister Alan Rock announced that the Canadian government would have cannabis grown in a Manitoba mine for distribution to patients, it seemed that the Canadians really would be the first to have a real program. But that was not to be.
See
Canadian Health Minister Seeks Asylum In DEAland; Says Making Her Think About Medical Cannabis Constitutes Torture. In DC They Don't Allow That Sort of Thing. Thinking, That Is.

Finally, as noted, the Dutch government decided to license private growers to provide supplies to pharmacies this year. The first licenses have been issued, and some are already in production, so it should not be much longer before the Dutch can claim victory in the medical cannabis sweepstakes. It remains to be seen whether they can keep up with demand, but that is another subject.

It is important to note that the Dutch government is also sponsoring research on the medical use of cannabis, while they are allowing distribution to patients and this does not violate the international treaties.
See
Swiss Government Says Going Dutch Does NOT Violate Treaties. Implications for Other Countries, Especially Canada and UK. Plus Full Text of UN Nark Press Release.
and links

Meanwhile back in Canada, the Health Ministry is hopelessly befuddled.

They now say that they are going to distribute the cannabis from the Manitoba mine to some of the patients in a research program. They are also allowing others to grow their own, but far more patients are being taken care of by the various Compassion Societies in the larger cities.

This is not quite analogous to the Dutch Mediwiet program, because the participating Dutch coffee shops were never in danger of being closed for selling medicine to the sick, which continues to be a problem for the Canadian Compassion Societies. But it is far better than nothing.

The key difference between the Dutch and the Canadian approaches is that the Dutch are allowing distribution to patients through pharmacies before the research is done, while Health Canada is insisting on having the research done first.

It would appear that the Canadians are putting science before compassion, but there is reason to question whether this is even good science.

The scientific problem is that they are not asking the right questions. It might seem that it would be very straightforward. After all, there is nothing new about testing drugs on patients. However, getting the right answers depends on asking the right questions.

Britannica defines science as any system of knowledge that is concerned with the physical world and its phenomena and that entails unbiased observations and systematic experimentation.

In the physical world as it actually exists there are already huge numbers of Canadians using cannabis therapeutically.
See
There Are Already Almost 600,000 Canadian Medical Marijuana Users, But Health Canada Has Only Approved 40 2 Articles With Interesting Lesson In Spin.

There are also thousands of people enrolled in the various Compassion Societies, who are using cannabis with some sort of medical supervision. It would be very easy to study these people and determine if they are having problems with cannabis. After all thousands of people die every year as a consequence of using even over-the-counter medicines that are generally accepted as safe. (GRAS, and ironically grass is not GRAS, by the government!)

It is important to understand that this sort of clinical use plays a major part in modern medical science, both in developing new drugs and determining the real-world safety of drugs after they have passed the FDA tests.
See
The Harsh Reality Of Clinical Trials
Shows Another Case of The Double Standard For Medical Marijuana.
The Context For " Research. " -- 2 Articles

Consequently, to delay formal distribution to patients until after the government has completed some sort of relatively limited research is ignoring a huge amount of data from sources that the government normally recognizes as valid when applied to other drugs. All that Health Canada would be doing is making scientific observation more limited and less complete than it could be. That is not good science.

Then there is the matter of ethics.

For example, it is considered unethical to continue to do standard double-blind placebo controlled research once it is determined that the patients who are receiving the drug being studied show significant benefit. It is already known that many people benefit from using cannabis.

Health Minister McLellan may claim that she does not know this, but it has been accepted as fact by both the US Institute of Medicine and the UK House of Lords Science and Technology committee and many other medical authorities.
See
Chairman of the House of Lords Science and Technology Committee
Criticizes UK Government's Rejection Of Report On Medical Marijuana
 2 Articles With 2 of the Worst Prohibitionist Arguments

It is also unethical to use a placebo when it is known that there are substances that benefit the patients.

That is, if a patient suffers from a condition that can be alleviated by a known substance, it is unethical to require that the patient forgo relief in order to test something. That problem is made more difficult for Health Canada if they continue to follow the practice of restricting research on cannabis to people who have already used cannabis and found it to be helpful. Thus, they are in the position of insisting that the patients who are given the placebo stop using something that the patients have already benefited from. That is unethical. The patients who are using the placebo would be the real guinea pigs, not the ones given cannabis.

But the ethical and scientific problems get even worse.

If a way is found around the problems noted above, there remains the problem of the context of cannabis prohibition.

It is unscientific to ignore the context in which the research is being done.

If science is any system of knowledge that is concerned with the physical world and its phenomena then it must take into consideration the fact that the legal harassment of patients is very much a part of the physical world and its phenomena.

If medicine is concerned with the well-being of the patients, then it is bad medicine and bad science to ignore the problems caused by prohibition.

Where are the studies on the side-effects of being arrested? Where are the studies of the effects of fear on patients? There are none, of course. But it is bad science to ignore these facts, which result from modern medicine as interpreted by Health Canada and the official medical establishment. It should not come as a surprise that they are reluctant to study the adverse consequences of their own policies. Who watches the watchman?

Does the Dutch parallel course (making cannabis available by prescription before the research is completed) offer a way out for Health Canada?

However, it should be noted that the Dutch Health Ministry is playing with a safety net. The coffee shops Mediwiet program will continue to be there take care of the patients while the new system is developed. The Canadian Compassion Societies have only a limited ability to do that, even if they are not harassed by the police.

Then there is the problem of the reluctant medical establishment. Canadian doctors have been frightened by threats from the professional associations and their own ignorance.
See
Cruelty, Incompetence, And Quackery Threaten Canadian Medical Cannabis Patients.
and
Lies Have Consequences. From Prohibitionist Venom to the Harsh Realities of Life and Death for Patients. Swedish Prohibitionists, Canadian Bureaucracy and DEAland Medical Murder.

The sad fact is that the medical establishments in virtually every country in the world, including the Netherlands, have proven themselves unworthy of trust and incapable of understanding the basics of science and ethics when dealing with cannabis.
